tier_reason: Peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2013 paper (docs/papers/asplos13.pdf, read in full) compares STOKE rewrites against gcc -O3 and icc -O3 output and OpenSSL's handwritten Montgomery kernel; Figure 1 caption and Section 1 state the Montgomery kernel is 16 lines shorter and 1.6x faster than gcc -O3 and slightly faster than the expert handwritten assembly. Not A: the paper gives no gcc/icc versions and does not name the machine that timed the kernels (only the 40-node 1.8 GHz AMD Opteron search cluster), and Figure 11's per-kernel speedups are chart-only.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper, Figure 1 caption and Section 1: the OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication kernel rewritten by STOKE is '16 lines shorter, 1.6x faster' than the gcc -O3 code 'and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly'. Abstract: STOKE's programs 'either match or outperform the code produced by gcc -O3, icc -O3, and in some cases, expert handwritten assembly'. Figure 11 plots speedups over llvm -O0 for Hacker's Delight p01-p25, saxpy, mont and list; per-kernel values appear only in the chart. The README's popcount tutorial times a loop at 1.046 s for g++ -O3 -fno-inline versus 0.133 s after STOKE patches popcnt() (about 7.9x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The paper is from 2013 and the speedups are on a small set of hand-picked loop-free kernels, plotted relative to llvm -O0 starting points in Figure 11; per-kernel numbers are chart-only, and the paper states no gcc/icc versions and does not name the timing machine. The README says 'We're not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code', calls STOKE a research prototype that 'isn't production ready', and says 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it needs gcc 4.9 to build. The README popcount tutorial's ~8x win compares against g++ -O3 without -march, so gcc cannot emit the popcnt instruction that STOKE uses; it shows the tool working, not a fair compiler comparison. The category fit (assembly tooling) is a judgement call: STOKE is a superoptimizer, and its baselines are compilers, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. The last commit (2020-12-04) only added a CodeQL workflow; the last code change is from 2019-10-03.

notes: Paper numbers match the record; tier B stands on the peer-reviewed ASPLOS paper. Shortcomings: hand-picked loop-free kernels, chart-only per-kernel speedups, no compiler versions or timing CPU, research prototype abandoned since 2019 (README says so), superoptimizer rather than an assembler, README popcount demo compares against -O3 without -march.

tier_reason: The only number is a README screenshot (imgs/aron-bm.png) of hyperfine -N --warmup 10 assembling test.macos.s, a 31-line clang -S output of a hello-world printf program: aron 3.9 ms vs macOS as 49.8 ms, 12.94 +/- 2.34x. With ~15 instructions of input both timings are process launch (macOS as is a driver that hands off to clang's integrated assembler), so the figure says nothing about assembly speed; the author calls it 'not empirical by any means', no CPU is named, and no output equivalence is checked. Downgraded to D following the wave 11 hop precedent (startup-dominated benchmark); it would be C on the bare rubric.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README screenshot (imgs/aron-bm.png) of 'hyperfine -N --warmup 10 "target/release/aron test.macos.s" "as test.macos.s"': aron 3.9 ms +/- 0.7 ms (777 runs) versus as 49.8 ms +/- 2.3 ms (60 runs), summary 'aron ... ran 12.94 +/- 2.34 times faster than as'. The README introduces it with 'This is not empirical by any means'.
corrections.workload: Assembling the repo's test.macos.s, a 31-line clang -S (Intel syntax) output of a hello-world printf program, once per process, with aron versus the macOS assembler; timings are dominated by process startup.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: aron built with cargo release profile (target/release); the screenshot's shell prompt shows rust v1.60.0 and C v13.1.6-clang (Apple clang 13.1.6 toolchain, which supplies the baseline as), aron v0.1.0; timed with hyperfine -N --warmup 10. No other flags stated.
corrections.hardware: A macOS machine; CPU model not stated.
corrections.caveats: The README says 'This is not empirical by any means'. One 31-line hello-world input (about 15 instructions), so both timings measure process launch rather than assembly: aron finishes in 3.9 ms while macOS as, a driver that hands off to clang's integrated assembler, takes 49.8 ms mostly in startup. No CPU is named, the output objects are not compared, and the assembler is self-described as incomplete, so the speedup also reflects its narrower feature set. The baseline is macOS as, not GNU as. The screenshot was taken on aron v0.1.0 (August 2022); the repo is now at 0.2.0. The language is Rust (Cargo.toml, edition 2021) although the repo page shows no language bar.

notes: Numbers on the README image match the record. Shortcomings: startup-dominated hello-world benchmark (31-line file), author disclaims it as not empirical, CPU unstated, no output check, incomplete assembler, 2 stars, abandoned since 2022-10-11. Downgraded C to D on the hop precedent; keep C instead if the orchestrator prefers the bare rubric.

tier_reason: First-party SGEMM wiki states 'as much as 25% over cublas' for small matrices (64-thread kernel) and 'At the 4096 size we're beating cublas by 4.8%' (256-thread kernel), 98% of theoretical on GM107 and 96% on GM204; GFLOPS exist only in chart images. The harness (sgemm/sgemm.cpp, sgemm.pl) is public but its cuBLAS timing calls are commented out, it builds as a Windows Visual Studio project, and no CUDA, cuBLAS or driver version or card model is given, so not A; no independent head-to-head found (maxDNN arXiv 1501.06633 reports 96% efficiency for a maxas-style SGEMM, snippet only, no cuBLAS comparison).

corrections.hardware: NVIDIA GM204 (Maxwell) at a sustained 1607 MHz core clock (1620 MHz boost scores excluded) with 8000 MHz memory; GM107 also cited for the 98% efficiency figure. Card model, driver, CUDA and cuBLAS versions are not stated on the page.
corrections.caveats: First-party wiki claim; exact per-size GFLOPS are only in chart images, and the page names no cuBLAS, CUDA or driver version, no card model and no flags. The public harness (sgemm/sgemm.cpp with sgemm.pl, a Windows Visual Studio build) has its cuBLAS timing code commented out, so the comparison cannot be rerun as published. The author says the kernels were 'derived from detailed study of the cublas Kepler and Maxwell sgemm implementations', and part of the gap comes from a cuBLAS bug that the wiki says costs cuBLAS sgemm 28 GFLOPS on GM204; the 2015-era cuBLAS has long since been superseded. The speedup is of a hand-scheduled SASS kernel against a library, not of the assembler against ptxas, GNU as, NASM or MASM; MaxAs only targets Maxwell (later partial half and dp4a support). Archived by the owner on 2023-01-03 with an Intel discontinuation notice; the last code commit is from 2016-06-10. Treat as a reference, not a general assembler win.

notes: Wiki numbers match the record (25% small-matrix, 4.8% at 4096, 98%/96% efficiency). Shortcomings: first-party, GFLOPS chart-only, no cuBLAS/CUDA versions or card model, cuBLAS comparison code commented out in the published harness, kernels derived from cuBLAS's own SASS plus a cuBLAS bug, archived 2023 (last code 2016).
